### Observed differences

- All six qualifying items concern resource allocation on six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22). In the earlier window, each activity's executions were concentrated on a consistent group of resources: one resource, User_49, alone held about 8–11 in 100 of the executions of every one of these activities, alongside several other resources each holding roughly 4–12 in 100. In the later window, User_49 no longer appears among the ten largest shares on any of these activities. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- In the later window, the largest individual shares belong to a largely different group: User_3, not among the largest shares earlier, holds about 8–9 in 100 of the executions of every affected activity. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- Allocation became less concentrated overall: the combined share of all resources outside the ten largest rose from roughly 28–44 in 100 earlier to roughly 39–51 in 100 later on every activity, an increase of about 6–11 in 100. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- A few resources keep a similar share in both windows; for example User_51 holds about 5–8 in 100 on each affected activity in both windows. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- Each allocation difference is 0.39–0.49 on a 0–1 dissimilarity scale and is larger than in about 1995 of 2000 random re-splits of the pooled traces; the profiles rest on 134–271 traces per window. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- No control-flow or timing evidence qualified (0 items against chance expectations of about 0.16 and 0.02), so no structural or timing difference is established. [screening]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility of a change in resource allocation: on activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, execution shifted from one group of resources that previously held the largest individual shares (including User_49) to a largely different group (including User_3), and the work became spread over more resources overall, with the share outside the ten largest resources rising by about 6–11 in 100 per activity. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Supporting signs: six resource items qualify where about 0.004 would be expected by chance for that family (roughly 1500 times the expectation), all six agree in direction — the same resources lose share while the same new group gains — each individual difference is larger than in about 1995 of 2000 random re-splits, and each profile rests on 134–271 traces per window. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, screening]

Limitations and competing explanation: the profiles for A13 and A14 are identical, so the six items describe five distinct activity profiles rather than six independent ones, and because much of the shift goes into the unnamed remainder the full set of gaining resources cannot be enumerated; a change in the mix of cases reaching these activities could also produce new resource shares without any reassignment of work, and with no qualifying control-flow or timing evidence this cannot be tested. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, screening]
